Mobile ground-to-air tracking platform

TALOS

A tracked robot that watches the sky.

Two drone sightings shut Gatwick for 33 hours in 2018. A thousand flights cancelled, 140,000 passengers stranded. Copenhagen lost four hours in 2025, and Munich lost a night. The equipment that finds the drone is priced for airports. This is the workbench version: a tracked chassis, a two-axis camera turret that holds a flying target on its own, and a receiver for the ID that every legal drone is required to broadcast, so the turret knows where to look before the camera has seen anything.

Why I built it

MISSION

I started with the part that looked hardest: keeping a camera pointed at something flying. That took three rewrites of the control loop, a tracker that remembers what the target looked like, and a chassis that turns when the turret runs out of room. It works. You click a flying object in the video feed and the turret holds it.

Then the flaw I had built in became obvious. Somebody has to click. The robot was blind until a human had already spotted the target, and a drone a couple of hundred metres out is a speck against a bright sky. By the time you can see it, it is already over whatever it came for. A tracker that needs to be told where to look is a demo, not a sensor.

So I went looking for how something this small could know about a drone before seeing it. Radar is out on price, licensing and complexity. Microphone arrays are still research projects. And then I found the thing that reframed the whole project: since 2024, in both the EU and the US, a drone is legally required to announce itself. It broadcasts an identifier, its position, its altitude and its pilot's location, in the clear, over Bluetooth and Wi-Fi, for anyone to receive. A chip that costs about 50 lei can hear it.

That turns Talos from a turret that tracks into a sensor that finds and then tracks, and it is the part nobody expects. Everything commercial in this space is either a stationary tripod camera or a cost-prohibitive UGV with a closed ecosystem. This is the accessible version: a Pi-class computer, off-the-shelf servos, and a chassis you can bolt anything onto.

The problem this fits

WHY IT MATTERS

A drone over a runway is not a nuisance, it is a stoppage. Nobody can prove the sky is clear, so everything stops until somebody decides it is. Gatwick lost 33 hours to two sightings in December 2018 and cancelled around a thousand flights. Copenhagen shut for roughly four hours in September 2025. Munich suspended flights the following month, and about three thousand passengers spent the night in the terminal.

The same pattern shows up wherever a small aircraft can reach something valuable. Drones drop phones and drugs into prison yards. There were 479 incidents in US federal prisons in 2024, up from 23 in 2018, and 1,712 recorded across England and Wales in a single year. They ground firefighting aircraft: the US Forest Service counted 218 drone incursions over wildfires in 2025, 184 of them over two fires, more than the previous seven years put together. Each one stops the water drops while the fire keeps moving.

It is not abstract here either. On 13 September 2025 a Russian Geran drone crossed into Romanian airspace during a strike on the Danube ports. Two F-16s went up from Fetești, RO-Alert went out across northern Tulcea county, and debris came down at Periprava, about a kilometre from the border. Romanian jets have been scrambled repeatedly since.

What all of these have in common is not firepower. It is knowing: what is up there, where it is, and whose it is. That is a sensor problem, and sensors can be cheap.

ROLE 01

Airfields

A sighting is a rumour until something confirms it. A unit that hears the broadcast and swings a camera onto it turns a rumour into a picture and a serial number.

ROLE 02

Prison yards

The drops happen at night, over the same few metres of wall, week after week. Cheap enough to park one on a roof, and it records what arrived and roughly where from.

ROLE 03

Fire and rescue

One hobby drone inside a restricted zone grounds every aircraft over the fire. This is mobile: it rides to the incident and watches the airspace the crews need.

ROLE 04

Restricted sites

Substations, ports, fuel depots, gas platforms. Fixed no-fly zones with long fences and nobody permanently watching the sky above them.

ROLE 05

Protected nature

Drone flights are restricted over reserves like the Danube Delta because they scatter nesting birds. Rangers currently find out when they hear one.

ROLE 06

Events

Stadiums, concerts and public gatherings get temporary no-fly zones and have no way to tell a licensed press drone from an unannounced one.

And what it honestly can't do. A drone that doesn't broadcast is invisible to the receiver: toy drones under 250 g, home-built FPV quads, and anything military. The Geran over Tulcea announced nothing. Those are exactly the cases where the camera has to earn its place, which is why tracking came first and stays the core of the project. Talos detects and tracks. It doesn't stop anything, and it isn't armed.

The question everybody asks: why not jam it? Technically the platform is already most of the way there. The hard half of any counter-drone system is finding the thing and keeping something pointed at it, and a transmitter is a small box. So the honest answer is that a jammer could be integrated, and deliberately isn't.

In Romania and across the EU, jamming equipment is banned outright: manufacturing, importing, owning, advertising, selling or using a device designed to cause harmful interference is prohibited and fined under Government Decision 740/2016, which ANCOM enforces. The reasoning is that a jammer doesn't only silence its target, it takes out everything nearby, including the calls somebody makes to the emergency number. In the US the FCC bans it under the Communications Act (sections 301, 302(b) and 333), with fines up to $112,500 per violation, and not even local police may use one. That authority sits with specific federal agencies. Interfering with an aircraft in flight is a separate and far more serious offence again.

Which means a jammer isn't a feature I left out for lack of time. In the hands of a student it would be illegal to own before it was ever switched on, and the legal version of this problem, telling an operator, a control room or a ranger what is up there and whose it is, is the part that was actually missing.

Sources: Gatwick 2018 · Copenhagen · Munich · Romania, F-16 scramble · Romanian incidents, EDMO · prison drops, CNN · National Institute of Justice · US Forest Service · FAA Remote ID enforcement · EASA & FAA Remote ID rules · ANCOM on jammers · FCC jammer enforcement

The first build

PROTOTYPE

I put the first Talos together for a freestyle robotics competition, the category with no fixed brief, where you turn up with whatever you built and explain why it should exist. It was made out of whatever was lying around: a tracked chassis, two 12 V motors wired to point in opposite directions, a Raspberry Pi, a pair of MG90S servos on a bracket, and a lithium pack soldered together by hand.

Most of it I decided in the last week. The turret bracket was sized to the servos that were in the box rather than the other way round. The tracking ran on a Flask page instead of an application because a browser was the fastest thing to put a video feed into, and the servo commands went out through an Arduino because that is what was already wired up.

It worked on the day. Not smoothly, but you could click a flying object in the video feed and watch the turret hold it, which was the whole argument. That was enough.

The interesting part is what happened afterwards: I didn't take it apart for the next project. Everything on this page is the second life of that prototype. The Arduino link became a PCA9685 on I²C, the Flask page became a FastAPI server and a PyQt6 application, CSRT became KCF with a colour memory behind it, the proportional-only servo loop became two clamped PID loops, and the chassis stopped being whatever was lying around and started being drawn in CAD.

The tracking

VISION

This was the hard part. A KCF correlation tracker does the frame-to-frame work, with MOG2 background subtraction running behind it to find things that move in the first place. On its own KCF loses the target constantly, especially when somebody walks between the camera and the thing you were following.

So the tracker also remembers what the target looked like. On the initial click it learns an HSV colour histogram of the region, and when KCF fails it back-projects that histogram over the frame to find the target again within a search radius around its last known position.

Three sanity checks reject the classic failure where the tracker quietly latches onto the wrong object: a box that jumps too far in one frame, a box that suddenly grows several times larger, or a patch whose colour has drifted too far from what was learned.

The state machine matters more than any single algorithm. While searching, the turret keeps sweeping in the direction the target was last travelling rather than stopping, which is usually where it reappears.

Turret & chassis assist

CONTROL

Two independent PID loops, one for pan and one for tilt, both driven by how far the target's centre sits from the centre of the image, in pixels. Not degrees, because the loop never knows the real-world angle to the target, only the error on the sensor.

The first version shook so hard it looked broken. Four things fixed it: the error is smoothed with an exponential moving average before it reaches the controller, the integral term is clamped so it cannot wind up while the target is occluded, errors under 12 px are treated as zero, and no single frame may move a servo more than 3.5°.

When the pan servo passes 30° off centre, the tracks spin the robot to bring the turret back toward the middle of its range. Early on this ping-ponged left and right forever, until hysteresis and a timeout stopped it.

Driving itself

AUTONOMY · WIP

A camera bolted to a tripod is a tripod. The reason Talos sits on tracks is that a target does not stay conveniently in front of you: it goes behind a building, behind a treeline, or simply out past the end of the turret's travel. Being able to move is what separates a fixed sensor from one that keeps working.

What works today is one piece of that: when the pan servo passes 30° off centre, the tracks rotate the robot to bring the turret back toward the middle of its range, with hysteresis and a timeout so it can't oscillate. The turret leads and the chassis follows. Everything else, actually going somewhere, is still a human on WASD or an Xbox controller.

What's in progress is closing that loop. The chassis has no idea where it is yet: no wheel odometry, no position feedback, and the lidar that would let it avoid obstacles is still synthesised in software. The GPS and IMU going on for Remote ID aiming are the same two sensors autonomy needs, which is convenient. Heading and position arrive once, and both features get to use them.

The order I plan to build it in: hold a heading while the turret tracks, then reposition on command without losing the target from frame, then obstacle avoidance from real lidar, then a patrol route it drives on its own while watching the sky. Each step is testable on its own, which is the only reason I think it's achievable. The version where a robot decides everything at once is how projects die.

Knowing where to look

REMOTE ID

Almost nobody knows this part, which is why it is the best thing in the project. Ask anyone and they will tell you a drone in the sky is anonymous. It isn't. Since 1 January 2024 in the EU, and enforced from 16 March 2024 in the US, a registered drone has to carry Remote ID and broadcast an identifier, its position, altitude, speed, heading and its pilot's location, unencrypted, over Bluetooth and Wi-Fi, several times a minute. It is a number plate you can read from a distance, and anyone is allowed to receive it.

An ESP32-C6 on the robot listens for those broadcasts, decodes them and passes them to the Jetson over USB. The Jetson subtracts the robot's own GPS position, turns the difference into a bearing and an elevation, takes away the robot's heading from the IMU, and slews the turret there.

Remote ID only gives a rough position. GPS is off by a few metres at both ends and the broadcast updates about once a second, which is too coarse to track with but good enough to get the drone into the camera frame. From there the existing tracker takes over. If the camera loses the target, the turret falls back to the Remote ID bearing.

This only works for drones that broadcast. Drones under 250 g and many home-built FPV quads don't, so the camera stays the main sensor. The receiver doesn't transmit anything. The project detects and tracks, nothing more.

Demonstrating it. The competition is held indoors at a stand, and GPS doesn't work indoors. So the live demo uses a stand-in drone: an ESP32 with a GPS module broadcasting a test ID at low power, mounted on a stick with a bright marker the camera can pick out. The receiver only reacts to that test ID, so other devices in the hall can't trigger it. When the broadcast is picked up the turret starts searching, the camera locks on, and whoever is holding the stick can walk it around. The full outdoor version, aimed by GPS, is shown on video.

The same shape, one size up

SCALED UP

When armies build the thing this project is a model of, they call it mobile counter-UAS, and the drawing looks familiar. The US Army's M-LIDS pairs two armoured vehicles: one carries the radar that detects and tracks, the other a remote turret with an electro-optical and infrared sensor on it. Northrop's M-ACE is a light truck with a mast holding 3D radar, radio-frequency sensors and cameras. DE‑M‑SHORAD is a Stryker with a 50 kW laser where the turret goes.

Strip the armour and the effector off any of them and what is left is a chassis that can move, a sensor that says something is out there, a turret that slews onto it, a camera that holds it, and a link to an operator. That is Talos, at 1:20 scale and on a student's budget. The detect-and-track half is the half that has to work before the other half means anything.

Where the war fits in. Ukraine spends its nights against Shahed and Geran one-way attack drones, and the problem there is arithmetic. A Patriot interceptor costs around $4.2 million, and the drone it kills costs roughly $20,000. A Gepard, a 1970s anti-aircraft gun, does the same job for a few thousand a burst, and a mobile fire group in a pickup with a thermal sight and a heavy machine gun does it for less. Against cheap mass, expensive defences lose even when they win.

The lesson that transfers here isn't the gun, it's where the cost hides. The cheap layer is not short of firepower, it is short of eyes: finding the thing at night, knowing where to look, and keeping something pointed at it while it moves. That is exactly what a $50 receiver, a $10 IMU and a camera on two servos are for, and it is why I kept the project on the sensor side.

And the limit, stated plainly. Remote ID is a civil aviation rule. A Shahed broadcasts nothing, and the drone that crossed into Tulcea announced nothing. Against military drones the Remote ID half of this design is worthless and only the camera and the infrared channel carry over. Talos is a prototype of the sensing pattern, not a weapon, and I'd rather say that than let the comparison do work it hasn't earned.

How the pieces talk

SYSTEM

A FastAPI server runs on the robot and a PyQt6 application runs on the operator's laptop. Video goes over plain MJPEG on two endpoints, and everything else rides one WebSocket.

The status block, with turret angles, pixel error, tracker state, motor speeds and the closest obstacle, is broadcast ten times a second. The lidar scan, which is far heavier, goes out five times a second on the same socket. The app sends back clicks, turret nudges, drive commands and resets.

How much of the robot's surroundings that scan will actually cover is still an open question. The unit isn't fitted yet, so what the radar draws today is a synthesised sweep standing in for a real one, and the scan area gets settled when the hardware does.

The operator app shows both camera feeds, a polar radar for the lidar, the status block and a drive pad. You can drive with WASD or an Xbox controller.

Every actuator has a simulated stand-in, so the whole stack runs on a laptop with no robot attached: the motors and servos just track what the numbers would be, the lidar is synthesised, and the cameras fall back to a test pattern.

Drawn, then cut

CAD

The competition chassis was an off-the-shelf tracked base with holes drilled where they were needed. The current one is drawn properly: a 223.2 × 120.0 mm tub that carries the drive motors, the pack and the electronics, with the turret mounting directly to the top face so the pan axis sits over the centre of rotation, which is what lets the chassis assist manoeuvre work without the target sliding across the frame while the robot turns.

Moving to a Jetson meant the compute no longer fits a Raspberry Pi footprint, so it gets its own plate: a 130.0 × 98.0 mm platform that matches the developer kit's mounting pattern on top and the chassis rails underneath, raised on ribs so there is air under the board and a channel for the camera and I²C runs. It was drawn against NVIDIA's own developer-kit model, 100.0 × 81.0 mm of carrier board, heatsink and connector stack, so the hole pattern and the clearances were right before anything was cut.

Hardware

BILL OF MATERIALS

On the robot today

ComputeRaspberry Pi 4B
ChassisTracked, 2 × 12 V DC
Motor driverL298N · 2 A/ch
Turret servos2 × MG90S metal gear
PWMPCA9685 · 16 ch · 12-bit
OpticsPi camera + IR sensor
Pack4S LiPo · ~14.8 V
Logic railBuck → 5 V / 3 A
Manual inputXbox controller

The motors sit on opposite sides wired in opposite directions, so the robot steers differentially, turning by running one track faster than the other. On top sits the pan–tilt turret: one servo rotates the camera horizontally, the other tilts it, which together covers the airspace above and around the robot.

Servo timing is deliberately offloaded to the PCA9685 over I²C rather than bit-banged on GPIO pins. Hardware PWM is the difference between a turret that holds an angle and one that buzzes.

Next platform: a Jetson Orin Nano with Jetson.GPIO for the motors, the same PCA9685 over I²C for the servos, and an IMX678 camera through GStreamer, plus a real RPLIDAR in place of the synthesised one. An ESP32-C6 on USB listens for Remote ID, and a GPS module with a BNO085 IMU gives the robot its own position and heading for aiming outdoors.

Things that went wrong

BUILD LOG

SymptomThe turret vibrated at rest

Raw pixel error straight into a proportional term meant every frame of sensor noise became a servo command. Fixed with an EMA on the error, a 12 px deadzone, and a 3.5° per-frame step clamp.

SymptomThe robot spun left–right forever

Chassis assist fired the moment pan crossed its threshold, which recentred the turret past the threshold in the other direction. Fixed with hysteresis on the trigger and a timeout on the turn.

SymptomThe tracker latched onto the wrong thing

Anything crossing the target's path could steal the correlation window. Fixed with three rejection tests: a 220 px jump limit, a 4.5× area-growth limit, and a colour-histogram distance check against what was originally clicked.

SymptomFast targets were lost for good

Once KCF failed there was nothing to recover with. Fixed with a SEARCHING state that back-projects the learned colour histogram within a 200 px radius of the last known position, and keeps sweeping the last known direction of travel.

SymptomServos jittered when the motors drew current

Logic and drive sharing one rail meant every acceleration browned out the controller. Fixed with a dedicated 5 V buck converter for logic and hardware PWM generation moved off the Pi entirely.

SymptomThe chassis crept while parked

Analog sticks never return to exactly zero. Fixed with a 0.15 deadzone on both joystick axes before anything reaches the motor driver.
